b9bc186d7d62062ba51a9d7690aa0aceff639762.summary: A 2018 security blog tutorial explaining how unquoted Windows service paths can be abused for local privilege escalation. It describes the general technique only and names no threat actor, campaign, malware, CVE, sector, country, or incident, so it is not a threat report.

b9b204ee5c8f664fe7d38868781eca75ede5d767.summary: This is a Snort intrusion-detection rule reference page for alert 1:26941, a MALWARE-CNC rule that fires on a download by a Win.Trojan.PipCreat RAT dropper. It gives a generic description of command-and-control alerts and standard rule boilerplate. Most sections read 'No information provided' or 'No public information', and it contains no threat analysis, attribution, or campaign detail.

b92b8343e8db6ce8482586f71dc322354502e6d8.summary: CrowdStrike's June 2021 report on how big game hunting ransomware groups changed in 2020. It describes data-leak extortion spreading across groups after November 2019, growth in dedicated leak sites, extra pressure tactics (email to victims, phone harassment, DDoS threats), tactics shared between groups, and the Maze Cartel collaboration formed in June 2020. It also covers ransomware that targets ESXi hosts and common exfiltration tools. The report ends with defensive advice on backups, multi-factor authentication, endpoint protection and calling for incident response help.

b9805bd188ebc18d211f2134dc18454c67feae44.summary: Unit 42 of Palo Alto Networks describes Xbash, a Linux and Windows malware family that combines a botnet, cryptocurrency mining, ransomware and self-propagation. On Linux it deletes databases on MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB servers and leaves a Bitcoin ransom note; the report found no recovery functionality. Self-propagation uses weak passwords, unpatched vulnerabilities and three known flaws in Hadoop, Redis and ActiveMQ. The report links Xbash to the Iron group (aka Rocke), which it calls likely. Four versions were found, activity dates from May 2018, and 48 incoming Bitcoin transactions…
